# bayome

**BAY**esian **O**ccurrence–abundance **M**icrobiome **E**stimation

bayome finds associations between microbial features (taxa, genes,
pathways) and sample metadata. For each feature it models the
**occurrence** (presence/absence) and the **abundance** together, links
the abundance effects to the occurrence effects, and **shares
information across features**, so that features with few observations
still get stable estimates and honest intervals. Every model is fitted
with the integrated nested Laplace approximation
([R-INLA](https://www.r-inla.org/)).

The arguments, formulas and output columns follow
[MaAsLin3](https://github.com/biobakery/maaslin3), so an existing
MaAsLin3 analysis runs by changing only the function name.

Website and worked example: <https://jmartinez-minaya.github.io/bayome/>

> **Status:** early development (version 0.0.0.9000). The default model
> (`shrinkage = "joint"`) and the default selection rule
> (`selection = "bh_lfsr"`) work and are tested on simulated data, not
> yet on real data.

## Installation

INLA is not on CRAN. Install it first:

``` r

install.packages(
  "INLA",
  repos = c(getOption("repos"),
            INLA = "https://inla.r-inla-download.org/R/stable"),
  dep = TRUE
)
```

Then install bayome from GitHub:

``` r

# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("jmartinez-minaya/bayome")
```

## Quick start

``` r

library(bayome)

fit <- bayome(
  input_data     = taxa,      # samples x features (or features x samples)
  input_metadata = meta,      # samples in rows
  output         = "bayome_output",
  formula        = ~ diagnosis + age + (1 | subject),
  exposure       = "diagnosis", # variable of interest; age is an adjustment
  reference      = "diagnosis,nonIBD"
)

fit
head(fit$results)
```

`output` gets `all_results.tsv` and `significant_results.tsv`. Use
`output = NULL` to keep the results in R only.

Plots (ggplot2 objects):

``` r

bm_plot_summary(fit)                              # top features, all coefficients
bm_plot_effects(fit, "diagnosisCD")               # effects with credible intervals
bm_plot_link(fit, "diagnosisCD")                  # prevalence vs abundance effects
bm_plot_association(fit, "Faecalibacterium_prausnitzii", "diagnosis")  # the data
```

The vignette (“Getting started with bayome”) runs the whole workflow on
the HMP2 inflammatory bowel disease data included in the package.

## The model

For each feature *j* and sample *i*, with *Y*_(ij) the normalised
abundance:

- **Prevalence** (all samples): logit P(*Y*_(ij) \> 0) = **x**_(i)’
  **β**_(j)^(prev) + random effects
- **Abundance** (samples where the feature is present): log₂*Y*_(ij) =
  **x**_(i)’ **β**_(j)^(abun) + random effects + ε_(ij)

Both parts are fitted together in one INLA call, with a binomial and a
Gaussian likelihood. Pre-processing: normalise (`TSS`, `CLR` or `NONE`),
filter, then transform (`LOG`, `PLOG` or `NONE`). Continuous covariates
are standardised by default.

### The default model (`shrinkage = "joint"`)

All features and both parts go into **one** INLA model. The model
distinguishes the **exposure** (`exposure = "diagnosis"`: the variable
of interest; by default the first variable of the formula) from the
**adjustment covariates** (all the others). For an exposure coefficient
*k* (for example `diagnosisCD`), the effect on feature *j* is split as:

- **Prevalence:** β_(jk)^(P) = μ_(k)^(P) + *u*_(jk)^(P), with
  *u*_(jk)^(P) ~ N(0, 2.5²) fixed: each feature is estimated from its
  own presence data, without pooling.
- **Abundance:** β_(jk)^(A) = μ_(k)^(A) + **λ_(k) · *u*_(jk)^(P)** +
  *e*_(jk), with *e*_(jk) ~ N(0, 1/τ_(k)) shared across features.

**λ_(k)** is one number per exposure coefficient, estimated from all
features: how much abundance tends to follow prevalence in these data. A
feature with few non-zero samples has its abundance effect shrunk
towards what its prevalence effect suggests, instead of towards zero.
When prevalence and abundance are unrelated, λ_(k) ≈ 0 and the model
reduces to an independent hierarchical abundance model.

Each **adjustment covariate** *l* (for example age or antibiotic use)
gets one effect per feature and part, γ_(jl) ~ N(0, 2.5²) with a fixed
prior: no pooling, no link and no extra hyperparameters. So the model
has two hyperparameters per exposure coefficient (λ_(k) and τ_(k)) plus
the variances of the random effects, however many adjustment covariates
there are. To give every covariate the full structure, list them all in
`exposure`.

Random effects of the formula (for example `(1 | subject)`) get one copy
per part, replicated per feature with a shared variance. Residual
variances are one per feature, estimated with `"vb"` (variational
updates with a common prior). The abundance effects are compared with
their median over features (compositional correction). The estimated λ
values are printed during the fit and stored in `fit$lambda`.

The alternatives are `shrinkage = "hierarchical"` (each part separately,
with a common prior for each) and `shrinkage = "none"` (each feature on
its own).

Priors are set with
[`bm_prior()`](https://jmartinez-minaya.github.io/bayome/reference/bm_prior.md):

| Component | Default prior |
|----|----|
| Fixed effects, prevalence | Normal(0, 2.5²) on the log-odds scale |
| Fixed effects, abundance | Normal(0, 10²) on the log₂ scale |
| Random-effect SDs | PC prior, P(σ \> 1) = 0.01 |
| [`ordered()`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/factor.html) random walk | PC prior, P(σ \> 1) = 0.01 |
| Between-feature SD (`"joint"`: abundance *e*; `"hierarchical"`: both parts) | PC prior, P(σ \> 1) = 0.01 (set with `bm_prior(random = )`) |
| Prevalence effect per feature *u*^(P) (`"joint"`) | Normal(0, 2.5²), fixed (no pooling; set with `bm_prior(fixed_sd_prevalence = )`) |
| Prevalence–abundance link λ (`"joint"`) | Normal(0, 1) |
| Adjustment covariate effect per feature γ (`"joint"`) | Normal(0, 2.5²), fixed, both parts (set with `bm_prior(adjustment_sd = )`) |
| `strata()` | iid effect with fixed, very small precision |

### Compositional correction

With relative abundances (TSS), when some features truly increase, all
the others appear to decrease. Each abundance coefficient is therefore
compared with the **median of that coefficient across features** instead
of with zero (`median_comparison_abundance = TRUE`, the default).

bayome does this on the posterior. For each coefficient and posterior
draw *s*:

- *m*^((s)) = median over features *j* of β_(j)^((s))
- δ_(j)^((s)) = β_(j)^((s)) − *m*^((s))

`lfsr`, `prob_positive` and the q-values then refer to δ, whose
posterior includes the uncertainty of the median. `coef` keeps the raw
coefficient unless `subtract_median = TRUE`. `null_hypothesis` reports
the median used. Draws are random: call
[`set.seed()`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/Random.html) first for
reproducible results.

### Sharing information across features

| `shrinkage` | Prevalence | Abundance | Link between parts |
|----|----|----|----|
| `"joint"` (default) | Each feature on its own (fixed N(0, 2.5²) prior) | Common prior across features, centred on λ·*u*^(P) | λ per covariate |
| `"hierarchical"` | Common prior across features, centred at 0 | Common prior across features (`hierarchical_reference`: μ or median) | None |
| `"none"` | Each feature on its own | Each feature on its own | None (or shared random intercepts with `link = "shared"`) |

With `"hierarchical"`, `hierarchical_variance` sets the residual
variances (`"vb"` by default, `"plugin"` from an
[`lm()`](https://rdrr.io/r/stats/lm.html) per feature, or `"estimated"`
inside INLA, which is much slower).

## Formula notation

Formulas are written in lme4-style notation and translated into INLA
internally.
[`bm_inla_formula()`](https://jmartinez-minaya.github.io/bayome/reference/bm_inla_formula.md)
shows the result of the translation.

| You write | Meaning | INLA term |
|----|----|----|
| `diagnosis + age` | Fixed effects | unchanged |
| `group(site)` | Categorical variable tested as a whole | fixed factor (joint inference: planned) |
| `ordered(stage)` | Ordered categorical; each level is compared with the previous one | `f(stage, model = "rw1")` (only with `shrinkage = "none"`) |
| `strata(pair)` | Matched designs (only one allowed) | `f(pair, model = "iid")` with fixed small precision |
| `(1 \| subject)` | Random intercept | `f(subject, model = "iid")` |
| `(age \|\| subject)` | Uncorrelated random intercept and slope | two `iid` terms |
| `(age \| subject)` | Correlated random intercept and slope | not supported yet |

The arguments `fixed_effects`, `random_effects`, `group_effects`,
`ordered_effects` and `strata_effects` also work when `formula` is not
given.

``` r

meta <- data.frame(diagnosis = factor(c("CD", "UC", "nonIBD", "CD")),
                   age = c(20, 35, 50, 41),
                   subject = c("a", "a", "b", "b"))
bm_inla_formula(~ diagnosis + age + (1 | subject), meta)
#> <bm_inla_model>
#> INLA formula:
#>   y ~ 1 + diagnosis + age + f(.bm_re_subject, model = "iid", hyper = .bm_hyper$random)
```

## Output

One row per feature, covariate level and model part:

| Column | Meaning |
|----|----|
| `feature`, `metadata`, `value`, `name` | Feature and coefficient |
| `coef` | Posterior mean |
| `stderr` | Posterior standard deviation |
| `lower_95`, `upper_95` | 95% credible interval |
| `prob_positive` | Posterior probability that the effect is positive |
| `lfsr` | Local false sign rate: probability that the sign of `coef` is wrong |
| `qval_individual` | Q-value within each coefficient and model part, from the `selection` rule |
| `lfsr_joint`, `qval_joint` | Association in at least one of the two parts |
| `null_hypothesis` | Reference the coefficient is compared with: the median across features under median comparison, otherwise 0 |
| `error` | Why a part was not fitted, or a warning about the estimate |
| `model` | `"prevalence"` or `"abundance"` |
| `N`, `N_not_zero` | Number of samples, and of samples where the feature is present |

There are no p-values.

### Selecting associations

`selection` turns the posteriors into `qval_individual` and `qval_joint`
(and `significant_results.tsv`):

| `selection` | Rule |
|----|----|
| `"bh_lfsr"` (default) | Benjamini–Hochberg on 2·lfsr within each coefficient and part; joint q-value from `pbeta(min(p), 1, 2)` then BH |
| `"rope"` | Probability that the corrected effect is practically null, P(\|effect\| ≤ `rope_delta`); q-value = running mean of the sorted probabilities |
| `"lfsr"` | Running mean of the sorted lfsr (Bayesian false sign rate) |

The lfsr is a sign-error probability. With continuous priors the
posterior puts no mass on “no effect”, so for null features it behaves
like a one-sided p-value. That is why the default applies
Benjamini–Hochberg to 2·lfsr, which controls the false discovery rate,
while the running-mean rules can let null features through when many
features have no effect.

Every rule is applied **separately for each coefficient** (for example
`diagnosisCD`): the multiple-testing family is “which features are
associated with this coefficient”. MaAsLin3 corrects all coefficients
together; then a covariate with many associations (such as sequencing
depth) lets null features of the exposure through.

## Main arguments

Data and model: `input_data`, `input_metadata`, `output`, `formula`,
`fixed_effects`, `random_effects`, `group_effects`, `ordered_effects`,
`strata_effects`, `reference`.

Filtering and pre-processing: `min_abundance`, `min_prevalence`,
`max_prevalence`, `zero_threshold`, `min_variance`, `normalization`,
`transform`, `standardize`.

Other: `max_significance`, `evaluate_only`, `save_models`, `cores`,
`verbosity`.

Bayesian settings:

- `shrinkage`: `"joint"` (default), `"hierarchical"` or `"none"`; see
  [Sharing information across
  features](#sharing-information-across-features). With `evaluate_only`,
  `"hierarchical"` is used instead of `"joint"`.
- `exposure`: the variable(s) of interest for `"joint"` (default: the
  first variable of the formula); the other covariates are adjustment
  covariates.
- `selection`: `"bh_lfsr"` (default), `"rope"` or `"lfsr"`, and
  `rope_delta` (default 0.5); see [Selecting
  associations](#selecting-associations).
- `prior`: priors, from
  [`bm_prior()`](https://jmartinez-minaya.github.io/bayome/reference/bm_prior.md).
- `hierarchical_reference`, `hierarchical_variance`, `int_strategy`:
  options of `shrinkage = "hierarchical"`.
- `link`: `"none"` (default) or `"shared"` (abundance random intercepts
  are a scaled copy of the prevalence ones; only with
  `shrinkage = "none"`).
- `n_draws`: posterior draws for the median comparison (default 4000; at
  most 1000 joint samples for `"joint"` and `"hierarchical"`).

Median comparison: `median_comparison_abundance`,
`median_comparison_prevalence`, `median_comparison_abundance_threshold`,
`median_comparison_prevalence_threshold` and `subtract_median`.

Unsupported arguments, such as plotting or `augment`, are accepted but
ignored, with a warning.

## Roadmap

Familiar interface and formula translation to INLA

Two-part hurdle model in a single INLA fit

Compositional correction: median comparison on posterior draws

Information sharing across features, with per-feature residual variances
estimated by `"vb"`

Joint prevalence–abundance model with an estimated link λ (`"joint"`,
default)

Selection rule that controls the FDR (BH on 2·lfsr, default)

Fully Bayesian selection with a spike-and-slab prior (posterior
probability of no effect, less bias on large effects)

Faster fits with subject effects

[`ordered()`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/factor.html) with `"joint"` and
`"hierarchical"`

Evaluation on real data

Joint inference for `group()` variables

Correlated random effects `(x | g)` (`iid2d` / `iidkd`)

Count likelihoods with sequencing depth as an offset

Plots

Vignette with the HMP2 example data

## Acknowledgements

The interface, the pre-processing steps, the two-part structure, the
median comparison and the output format follow
[MaAsLin3](https://github.com/biobakery/maaslin3) (Nickols, Nearing et
al., Huttenhower lab), distributed under the MIT license. bayome is an
independent package, not part of MaAsLin3 or bioBakery. If you use
bayome, please also cite MaAsLin3:

> Nickols WA, Kuntz T, Shen J, Maharjan S, Mallick H, Franzosa EA,
> Thompson KN, Nearing JT, Huttenhower C. MaAsLin 3: refining and
> extending generalized multivariable linear models for meta-omic
> association discovery. *Nature Methods* 23, 554–564 (2026). doi:
> [10.1038/s41592-025-02923-9](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41592-025-02923-9)

# Package index

## Fitting models

- [`bayome()`](https://jmartinez-minaya.github.io/bayome/reference/bayome.md)
  : Bayesian occurrence-abundance microbiome estimation
  (MaAsLin3-compatible)
- [`bm_prior()`](https://jmartinez-minaya.github.io/bayome/reference/bm_prior.md)
  : Priors for bayome models

## Plots

- [`bm_plot_summary()`](https://jmartinez-minaya.github.io/bayome/reference/bm_plot.md)
  [`bm_plot_effects()`](https://jmartinez-minaya.github.io/bayome/reference/bm_plot.md)
  [`bm_plot_link()`](https://jmartinez-minaya.github.io/bayome/reference/bm_plot.md)
  [`bm_plot_association()`](https://jmartinez-minaya.github.io/bayome/reference/bm_plot.md)
  : Plot bayome results

## Formulas

- [`bm_parse_formula()`](https://jmartinez-minaya.github.io/bayome/reference/bm_parse_formula.md)
  : Parse a MaAsLin3-style formula
- [`bm_compose_formula()`](https://jmartinez-minaya.github.io/bayome/reference/bm_compose_formula.md)
  : Build a MaAsLin3-style formula from separate effect arguments
- [`bm_inla_formula()`](https://jmartinez-minaya.github.io/bayome/reference/bm_inla_formula.md)
  : Translate a parsed formula into an INLA model

## Selection

- [`bm_qvalue()`](https://jmartinez-minaya.github.io/bayome/reference/bm_qvalue.md)
  : Bayesian q-values from local false sign rates
